hook: The warrior queen of Britain who burned Roman London.

pages.x: Boudica was the wife of Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, a Celtic people of eastern Britain. A Roman writer described her as very tall, with a harsh voice and a mass of red hair down to her hips, wearing a heavy gold necklace and a many-coloured cloak.

When Prasutagus died around AD 60, he left half his kingdom to the Roman emperor, hoping to protect his family. Instead Roman officials seized everything. Boudica was flogged, and her two daughters were raped.

With the Roman governor away in Wales, Boudica raised the Iceni and their neighbours. They burned Colchester, the Roman capital, then London and St Albans, killing perhaps 70,000 people. Under London, archaeologists still find a layer of red, burned earth from her attack.

The governor marched back with about 10,000 soldiers and chose his ground in a narrow valley. Boudica's huge army charged, but was cut to pieces; the Romans claimed 80,000 dead. Boudica is said to have taken poison rather than be captured.

For centuries she was almost forgotten. Then the Roman histories were rediscovered, and in Queen Victoria's time Boudica became a national heroine. In 1902 a bronze statue of her in a chariot with scythes on its wheels was put up beside the Houses of Parliament.
Boudica's revolt nearly drove the Romans out of Britain. She became a symbol of resistance to invaders, and of a woman leading her people into battle.
pts: Led a great revolt against Roman rule
A British symbol of courage and freedom
